metadata.title: CARDIOVASCULAR SYSTEM (CVS) OSCE
metadata.subtitle: 15 Evidence-Corrected Stations
metadata.audienceAndScoring: Final-Year MBBS • 10 minutes per station • 20-point analytic checklist
metadata.facultyNote: This manual contains exactly 15 standalone final-year MBBS cardiovascular OSCE stations, written for KMU-pattern final-year MBBS and postgraduate (CPSP) examinations. Stations 1–5 are clinically revised versions of the candidate's own supplied CVS teaching material (chest pain/MI, angina, post-MI counselling and medication advice, hypertension, atrial fibrillation); stations 6–15 broaden coverage across heart failure, conduction/rhythm emergencies, endocarditis, thromboembolic disease, valvular/rheumatic heart disease, lipid management, and cardiac arrest. Local protocols supersede imported guidance. NICE, ESC/EACTS, and Resuscitation Council UK recommendations are used as identified evidence standards. They do not create Pakistani legal, licensing, prescribing, referral, or service obligations. Faculty must replace imported operational details with the current approved institutional, provincial, and national protocols before summative use. Resource constraints may shape implementation but must not reduce emergency safety.
assessmentDesign: Each station is designed for 10 minutes and uses a 20-point analytic checklist (10 observable items scored 0, 1, or 2).
Score 2 = clearly and independently achieved; 1 = partially achieved or achieved only after a standard prompt; 0 = omitted, incorrect, or unsafe.
The analytic score and global rating must be recorded independently. No numerical pass mark is prescribed; use an approved standard-setting process.
Critical safety errors require examiner review and may justify failure when they create material danger. A minor omission alone should not automatically fail a candidate.
Candidate learning notes are intended for release after the station unless faculty deliberately uses the page for formative open-book teaching.
Standardised prompts restore progress without revealing the answer. Record every prompt and apply the same scoring rule to every candidate.
printingAndAssembly: Each station begins on a new page. Candidate-facing material precedes a marked "Examiner confidential" break.
Remove or cover the Learning Note paragraph if the handout is used during a summative station.
Verify medicines, emergency charts, laboratory reference ranges, referral contacts, and equipment against the local site before use.
contents: 1. Acute Coronary Syndrome / Acute MI — History, ECG interpretation, and emergency GP-level management
2. Stable Angina — History, differential diagnosis, and secondary-prevention counselling
3. Post-MI Secondary Prevention — Lifestyle, medication counselling, and return-to-activity planning
4. Hypertension — Counselling on lifestyle and stepped drug therapy
5. Atrial Fibrillation — History, stroke-risk assessment, and management planning
6. Chronic Heart Failure — Management review and guideline-directed drug therapy
8. Bradyarrhythmia / Complete Heart Block — Acute-management simulation
10. Infective Endocarditis — History, examination, and referral planning
11. Deep Vein Thrombosis — Data interpretation and counselling
13. Rheumatic / Valvular Heart Disease (Mitral Stenosis) — Examination and counselling

stations.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome / Acute MI
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused chest-pain history, ECG interpretation, and emergency GP-level management
candidateInstructions: You are a GP. Mr Allah Rakha, aged 51 years, presents with severe central chest pain for the last 10 minutes.

In 10 minutes: take a focused pain history (onset, site, character, radiation, associated features, relieving/aggravating factors, medicines, prior investigation), interpret the supplied ECG finding, and manage him as an emergency.
You do not need to draw the ECG yourself — interpret the handout description. Do not delay emergency transfer to complete a full social history.
candidateHandout: Pain: constant, severe (7–8/10), central chest and left arm to the little finger, started while walking uphill carrying groceries; associated nausea and profuse sweating; not relieved by rest or over-the-counter paracetamol.
ECG (already performed): changes consistent with anterior myocardial infarction.

Risk factors on request: heavy smoker (2 packs/day), regular alcohol use, father died of a heart attack, no known diabetes; significant psychosocial stress (job insecurity, recent marital separation).
learningNotes: Learning note (release after the station): Suspected ACS with ischaemic ECG changes needs immediate emergency-department transfer for reperfusion assessment — time to thrombolysis/PCI is the single biggest determinant of myocardial salvage. Pre-transfer GP-level measures under NICE NG185 are aspirin 300 mg chewed/dispersed immediately (unless a genuine contraindication or already taken), analgesia (IV opiate such as morphine, with an antiemetic such as metoclopramide), oxygen only if SpO2 is low, IV access, and arranging the fastest safe transfer with a written medicines record for the receiving team. GTN does not replace opioid analgesia in an evolving MI and does not by itself confirm or exclude a cardiac cause.
simulationScript: Opening: "Doctor, I have severe chest pain, like a heavy weight on my chest, and I'm short of breath." Appear distressed and diaphoretic but able to answer questions.

If asked about the pain (OD-PARA-MI/SOD-PARRA-MI style): as in the handout — constant, severe, central with left-arm radiation, worse with exertion, relieved somewhat by rest, associated nausea and sweating, no relief with paracetamol.

Differential screening answers: no pleuritic component, no recent long-haul travel or immobilisation, no leg swelling, no chest trauma, no unilateral vesicular rash, pain is not reproducible with one-finger palpation or movement, not relieved by antacid, no difficulty swallowing.
Red flags: no weight loss, no fever, no night sweats, no haemoptysis.
If asked for the ECG: state "changes consistent with anterior myocardial infarction" — do not require the candidate to read raw ECG paper.
ICE: frightened of dying; has a flight booked in a few hours to see a new grandchild and initially resists admission; accepts admission once the candidate explains the risk in plain, honest language.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. If the candidate offers analgesia before completing the full history, that is good practice, not a deduction.

Full marks for management require, at minimum: aspirin 300 mg immediately, adequate analgesia (opioid ± antiemetic), oxygen only if hypoxic (do not reward routine high-flow oxygen in a non-hypoxic patient — this is an outdated and now discouraged practice), IV access, and an explicit statement of urgent ambulance transfer to a facility capable of reperfusion.
If the candidate proposes discharge, delay, or letting the patient fly, this is a critical safety error regardless of other performance.
Prompted items score at most 1/2. Record every prompt.
keyAnswerGuide: Take a focused, open pain history using a structured mnemonic (onset, site, character, radiation, associated features, relieving/aggravating factors, medicines, investigations) while continuously observing for haemodynamic compromise.
Screen and verbalise the chest-pain differential (musculoskeletal, pericarditis, dissection, PE, pneumothorax, oesophagitis, shingles) and explain why each is against the presentation.
Interpret the ECG description as anterior MI and recognise this as a time-critical emergency.

Give aspirin 300 mg, opioid analgesia with antiemetic, oxygen only if indicated, IV access, and arrange immediate emergency transfer; provide a written summary of medicines given to avoid duplication in the receiving unit.
Address the patient's understandable reluctance (the flight) with honest, values-based communication rather than coercion, and gain informed agreement to transfer.
suggestedApproach: Open, listen, and assess severity/haemodynamic status early.
Take a structured pain history and screen red flags/differentials.
Interpret the ECG finding and recognise the emergency.
Give immediate evidence-based pre-transfer treatment.
Explain the diagnosis honestly and negotiate urgent transfer.
Document and hand over safely.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self, confirms identity, and opens with an invitation to describe the pain.
Takes a structured pain history: onset, site, character, radiation, severity, timing.
Elicits associated features (nausea, sweating, breathlessness) and relieving/aggravating factors.
Screens the chest-pain differential (PE, pneumothorax, pericarditis, dissection, shingles, musculoskeletal, oesophageal) with targeted questions.
Screens red flags (weight loss, fever, night sweats, haemoptysis) and cardiac risk factors (smoking, alcohol, family history, diabetes).
Correctly interprets the supplied ECG description as anterior MI and recognises the emergency.
Gives aspirin 300 mg immediately (unless a genuine contraindication).
Gives adequate analgesia (opioid) with an antiemetic, and oxygen only if hypoxic.
Secures IV access and arranges immediate emergency transfer without delay.
Communicates honestly and sensitively, addresses the patient's own priority (the flight), and documents/hands over safely.

globalRating: Clear fail — Unsafe, disorganised, or unable to achieve the core task despite prompts.
Borderline — Partial achievement with important omissions; may require prompts but avoids major harm.
Pass — Safe, structured, clinically appropriate performance with minor omissions.
Good — Efficient, patient-centred, well-reasoned performance with clear prioritisation.
Excellent — Fluent integration of clinical reasoning, communication, safety-netting, and context without irrelevant overreach.
promptQuestions: "What immediate treatment would you give before the ambulance arrives?"
"How would you explain the urgency to a patient who wants to leave for a flight?"
"What would change your management if the patient became hypotensive?"
criticalSafetyErrors: Delays or omits aspirin without a genuine contraindication.
Gives routine high-flow oxygen to a non-hypoxic patient, or omits oxygen when hypoxia is present.
Allows discharge, delay, or unsupervised travel in suspected acute MI.

NICE QS68 — Acute coronary syndromes in adults (quality standard). https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs68 Accessed September 2026. stations.title: Stable Angina
stations.primaryCompetency: Structured pain history, differential diagnosis, and stepwise secondary-prevention counselling
candidateInstructions: Mr Ashraf Butt, known to have had an MI last year, presents with chest pain that is now more frequent, more severe, and longer-lasting despite his GTN spray.
In 10 minutes: take a structured pain history, screen for unstable features, examine as directed by the handout, and counsel on lifestyle and drug secondary prevention.
Do not quote a fixed dose escalation beyond what the handout/answer guide supports; individualise to heart rate/BP response.
candidateHandout: Pain: central, crushing, radiates to neck and left arm, brought on by cold, emotion, heavy meals, and exertion; relieved by rest and GTN spray within 10–15 minutes; frequency and severity have increased over recent weeks; no episode has yet lasted more than 15 minutes.
Examination on request: heart sounds normal in all four areas, chest clear, BP and pulse within acceptable range, no signs of heart failure.

Past history: previous MI; heavy smoker (wants to quit); occasional alcohol; strong family history of ischaemic heart disease and hypertension; no known diabetes; is a cashier (a sedentary, stressful job).
learningNotes: Learning note: This is stable angina until proven otherwise, but any pain lasting over 15 minutes despite rest and GTN, pain at rest, or rapidly crescendo pain is unstable angina and needs urgent cardiology referral/admission. NICE CG126 (Stable angina: management) supports GTN spray for acute attacks, a first-line anti-anginal (commonly a beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker), and secondary-prevention aspirin, a statin, and an ACE inhibitor where indicated. Beta-blockers are avoided or used cautiously in reactive airway disease.
simulationScript: Opening: "Doctor, since my heart attack I've had chest pain on exertion which used to settle with my spray, but now it's more frequent and lasts longer."
If asked (SOD-PARRA-MI): as per handout; confirms no episode has exceeded 15 minutes; no pain at rest so far.
Differential screening: pain is not reproducible by palpation, not worse on movement or breathing, no antacid relief, no chest trauma, not worse lying flat, not relieved by sitting forward.
Personal/social: heavy smoker, intends to stop; drinks occasionally, intends to cut down; significant work and home stress; not known to be asthmatic (confirm on request).
ICE: fears another heart attack; hopes for medicine beyond the spray; worried about being told he needs surgery.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. Provide examination findings only on request, as listed in the handout.

Full marks require the candidate to explicitly screen for "unstable" features (rest pain, crescendo pattern, pain >15 minutes) and state that any of these requires urgent same-day cardiology assessment rather than routine anti-anginal titration.

Accept any safe drug sequence consistent with local formulary; beta-blocker first-line is standard but calcium-channel blocker is an acceptable alternative, particularly if reactive airway disease is present.
keyAnswerGuide: Take a structured pain history, confirm the pattern remains "stable" (exertional, relieved by rest/GTN, no episode >15 minutes), and screen the chest-pain differential.
Examine heart sounds, lungs, BP, and pulse; order ECG, FBC, fasting lipid profile, cardiac enzymes only if an acute event is suspected, fasting glucose, ESR, and TFTs as first-line work-up.

Explain the pathophysiology in plain language and counsel on smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, diet, weight, structured exercise within symptom limits, and driving/occupational restrictions relevant to his job.

Offer GTN spray technique review (repeat after 5 minutes, call an ambulance after a second repeat dose or if pain persists), a first-line anti-anginal (beta-blocker, e.g. atenolol, titrated to resting heart rate around 60 beats/min, avoided/cautious in asthma; calcium-channel blocker such as amlodipine as an alternative or add-on; long-acting nitrate as a further step), and secondary prevention with aspirin (or clopidogrel if aspirin-intolerant), a statin, and an ACE inhibitor.
Safety-net: any pain lasting over 15 minutes despite rest and GTN, or pain at rest, is a medical emergency requiring an ambulance, not a routine follow-up appointment.
suggestedApproach: Elicit the pain pattern and confirm it remains exertional/stable.
Screen differentials and red flags for instability.
Examine and investigate as indicated.
Explain the diagnosis and negotiate a stepped management plan.
Cover lifestyle, driving, and psychosocial factors.
Safety-net for unstable angina and check understanding.

checklist.criterion: Opens with rapport and elicits a structured, chronological pain history.
Confirms exertional pattern, relief with rest/GTN, and screens explicitly for rest pain/crescendo pattern/duration >15 minutes.
Screens the chest-pain differential (musculoskeletal, pericarditis, oesophageal, pneumothorax) with targeted questions.
Reviews cardiac risk factors: smoking, alcohol, family history, diabetes, and occupational/psychosocial stress.
Requests/interprets a focused examination (heart sounds, chest, BP, pulse) appropriately.
Orders appropriate first-line investigations (ECG, lipids, glucose, FBC ± TFT/ESR) without over-investigating.
Explains angina pathophysiology in plain, patient-centred language.
Reviews GTN spray technique and gives the correct emergency escalation rule (repeat dose, call ambulance after second repeat/persistent pain).
Proposes an individualised first-line anti-anginal plus secondary-prevention aspirin/statin/ACE inhibitor, checking for asthma before beta-blockade.
Explicitly safety-nets for unstable angina and addresses driving/occupational and psychosocial concerns.

globalRating: Clear fail — Unsafe, disorganised, or unable to achieve the core task despite prompts.
Borderline — Partial achievement with important omissions; may require prompts but avoids major harm.
Pass — Safe, structured, clinically appropriate performance with minor omissions.
Good — Efficient, patient-centred, well-reasoned performance with clear prioritisation.
Excellent — Fluent integration of clinical reasoning, communication, safety-netting, and context without irrelevant overreach.
promptQuestions: "What features would make you treat this as unstable angina instead?"
"What would you check before starting a beta-blocker?"
"What should the patient do if the spray doesn't work?"
criticalSafetyErrors: Fails to screen for or recognise unstable-angina features.
Prescribes a beta-blocker without checking for asthma/reactive airway disease.
Gives no clear emergency-escalation instruction for the GTN spray.

stations.title: Post-MI Secondary Prevention
stations.primaryCompetency: Lifestyle counselling, medication explanation, and return-to-activity planning after myocardial infarction
candidateInstructions: Mr Muhammad Mahmood was discharged 7 days ago after an MI. He has come for his post-discharge counselling visit.

In 10 minutes: explain the diagnosis in plain language, counsel on lifestyle (diet, exercise, weight, smoking, alcohol, driving, flying, sexual activity, psychological effects), and explain his secondary-prevention medicines and their safety-netting.
Do not promise he will never have another heart attack; be honest while reassuring.
candidateHandout: Current medicines: aspirin, a beta-blocker (atenolol), an ACE inhibitor (ramipril), a statin (simvastatin), and a GTN spray for emergency use.
No current chest pain, breathlessness, fever, or pleuritic pain (screen for Dressler syndrome).
Occupation: a desk-based (sedentary) job; enjoys swimming; is a smoker; drinks socially.
learningNotes: Learning note: NICE CG172 (MI: cardiac rehabilitation and secondary prevention) supports a graded return to activity (rest briefly, then gradually increasing walking distance over 4–6 weeks), cardiac rehabilitation referral, smoking cessation support, dietary advice (Mediterranean-pattern diet, oily fish, reduced salt/saturated fat), and driving/flying guidance following local and licensing-authority rules. Fever, pleuritic chest pain, or a pericardial rub 2–10 weeks after MI suggests Dressler syndrome and needs cardiology referral. Depression is common (roughly half of patients in the first week, around a quarter at one year) and should be actively screened for.
simulationScript: Opening: "Doctor, I'm glad to be home, but I have a lot of questions about what I can and can't do now."

Questions the patient may ask if given the opportunity: "What exactly is a heart attack?" "Can I have another one?" "What is an angiogram / treadmill test?" "When can I go back to work?" "When can I fly?" "When can I have sex again?"
If asked about mood: admits feeling low and anxious since discharge, worried about dying suddenly; no suicidal ideation.
If asked about the medicines: willing to take them but worried about side effects, especially impotence, and asks whether he really needs all four.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. Expect the candidate to structure counselling rather than deliver an unstructured monologue.

Full marks require an explicit, graded return-to-activity plan (not just "take it easy"), explicit driving/flying guidance, a depression screen, and safety-netting for Dressler syndrome and medicine-specific danger symptoms (aspirin bleeding, statin muscle pain, ACE-inhibitor cough/angioedema, beta-blocker bradycardia/hypotension).
Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Explain MI in plain language (blocked heart-vessel blood supply causing muscle death, replaced by scar over 4–6 weeks) and answer the patient's specific questions (angiography, exercise tolerance test) honestly.

Give a graded activity plan: brief rest, short walks, gradually increasing distance/pace over 4–6 weeks; occupation-dependent return to work (sooner for sedentary work, later for heavy manual labour); swimming after 4–6 weeks; driving restriction for about a week with a formal fitness assessment; flying restriction for about 2 weeks and only once able to climb stairs without symptoms; sexual activity generally after some weeks once exercise tolerance allows, avoiding heavy meals/hot baths beforehand, and never combining a GTN spray with a PDE5-inhibitor such as sildenafil because of dangerous hypotension.
Address diet (reduce salt/saturated fat, increase fruit/vegetables/oily fish), weight, smoking cessation (offer support/referral), and safe alcohol limits.

Explain each secondary-prevention medicine (beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, aspirin, statin, GTN) with its purpose, common side effects, and a clear safety-netting instruction for each; never suggest stopping any of them abruptly on the patient's own initiative.
Screen for depression and for Dressler syndrome; arrange follow-up and cardiac rehabilitation referral.
suggestedApproach: Open, acknowledge the recent event, and invite questions.
Explain the diagnosis and answer specific questions.
Cover a graded activity/return-to-work/driving/flying/sex plan.
Cover diet, weight, smoking, and alcohol.
Explain each medicine with safety-netting.
Screen mood, safety-net for Dressler syndrome, and arrange follow-up.

checklist.criterion: Opens supportively and structures the consultation around the patient's own questions and concerns.
Explains MI and its natural history in clear, non-technical language.
Gives a graded, staged return-to-activity plan (rest, walking distance, timeframe).
Gives occupation-appropriate return-to-work guidance and correct driving and flying restrictions.
Addresses sexual activity, including the GTN/PDE5-inhibitor interaction warning.
Covers diet, weight, smoking cessation support, and alcohol moderation.
Explains each secondary-prevention medicine's purpose and does not suggest self-directed stopping.
Gives medicine-specific safety-netting (bleeding, muscle pain, cough/angioedema, bradycardia/hypotension).
Actively screens for depression/psychological effects.
Safety-nets for Dressler syndrome and arranges cardiac rehabilitation/follow-up.

globalRating: Clear fail — Unsafe, disorganised, or unable to achieve the core task despite prompts.
Borderline — Partial achievement with important omissions; may require prompts but avoids major harm.
Pass — Safe, structured, clinically appropriate performance with minor omissions.
Good — Efficient, patient-centred, well-reasoned performance with clear prioritisation.
Excellent — Fluent integration of clinical reasoning, communication, safety-netting, and context without irrelevant overreach.
promptQuestions: "When can he safely return to work and to driving?"
"What would make you suspect Dressler syndrome?"
"What must never be combined with a GTN spray, and why?"
criticalSafetyErrors: Fails to warn against combining GTN spray with a PDE5-inhibitor.
Gives no graded activity plan, or clears the patient for unrestricted activity/driving/flying immediately.
Misses or dismisses a depression screen or Dressler-syndrome safety-netting.

stations.title: Hypertension
stations.primaryCompetency: Diagnosis explanation, lifestyle counselling, and stepped antihypertensive therapy
candidateInstructions: Mr Fazal Ahmad, aged 57 years, has had repeatedly high blood pressure readings on separate occasions. He feels well but is low in mood and reports erectile difficulty.
In 10 minutes: confirm the diagnosis in plain language, screen for end-organ damage and secondary causes, counsel on lifestyle change, and offer stepped drug therapy with side-effect counselling.
Do not invent a numeric age-based rule beyond the supplied NICE-style step algorithm.
candidateHandout: Readings: persistently elevated on multiple occasions over the past year; secondary-cause screening tests already performed are negative.
No known heart, cerebrovascular, renal, or visual end-organ damage on direct questioning; occasional headache and blurred vision were the only symptoms, found incidentally.
Personal: smoker; drinks beyond recommended limits; sedentary desk job; overweight; not known diabetic.
learningNotes: Learning note: NICE NG136 defines a stepped approach — under 55 years (and not of Black African/African-Caribbean family origin) start with an ACE inhibitor or ARB (A); 55 and over, or of Black African/African-Caribbean family origin at any age, start with a calcium-channel blocker (C); step 2 combines A+C or A+D; step 3 combines A+C+D, where D is a thiazide-like diuretic; a beta-blocker or alpha-blocker is considered as a further add-on step, particularly in younger patients or those with specific indications. Target is generally below 140/90 mmHg (below 130/80 if diabetic), individualised by age and frailty. Beta-blockers and diuretics can cause or worsen erectile dysfunction and low mood — this is directly relevant to this patient's presenting concerns.
simulationScript: Opening: "But doctor, I feel fine — do I really need medicine?"
If asked: diagnosed incidentally about a year ago; occasional headache/blurred vision only; no chest pain, breathlessness, leg swelling, or prior stroke; no known kidney or urinary problem.
Personal/social: smoker, heavy drinker, sedentary job, overweight, minimal exercise; family history of hypertension and heart disease.
Mood/sexual: admits low mood and erectile difficulty; asks whether the tablets themselves might make this worse.
ICE: fears this is untreatable and lifelong; worried about a friend who died of high blood pressure; wants to know how to live normally and avoid complications.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. If the candidate performs examination, state BP confirmed elevated on repeat, fundoscopy normal, heart and lungs unremarkable.

Full marks require the candidate to name the correct first step by the supplied age rule, and to explicitly connect the mood/erectile-dysfunction concern to a rational drug choice (e.g., avoiding or later reviewing a beta-blocker/diuretic, offering an ACE inhibitor/ARB or calcium-channel blocker as more mood/sexual-function-neutral options).
Accept any safe, locally available option within the correct drug class. Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Confirm the diagnosis of essential hypertension after excluding secondary causes and screen for end-organ damage (cardiac, cerebrovascular, renal, visual) and diabetes.
Explain the condition and that it is controllable, not curable, requiring ongoing treatment even when asymptomatic.

Counsel on salt/fat reduction, increased fruit/vegetable intake, reduced alcohol, smoking cessation, regular exercise, and weight reduction; discourage unsupervised calcium/magnesium/potassium supplements as a substitute for treatment.

Select the first-line drug by the supplied age/ethnicity rule (ACE inhibitor/ARB under 55; calcium-channel blocker at 55+ or Black African/Caribbean family origin), and explain stepped add-on therapy if control is not achieved.

Explicitly discuss side effects relevant to this patient — beta-blockers and thiazide diuretics can cause or worsen depression and erectile dysfunction, so an ACE inhibitor/ARB or calcium-channel blocker is a more suitable choice here; note ACE-inhibitor contraindications (pregnancy, cough) and calcium-channel blocker side effects (ankle oedema, flushing).
Arrange baseline investigations (renal function/electrolytes, lipid profile, glucose, urine protein, ECG), follow-up, and safety-netting for new symptoms.
suggestedApproach: Confirm diagnosis and screen for secondary causes/end-organ damage.
Explore lifestyle, mood, and sexual-function concerns.
Explain the condition honestly.
Counsel on lifestyle modification.
Choose and explain a first-line drug appropriate to age and to the mood/sexual-function concern.
Arrange investigations, follow-up, and safety-netting.

checklist.criterion: Builds rapport and explores the patient's own understanding and concerns first.
Confirms the diagnosis was made on repeated readings and screens for secondary causes.
Screens for cardiac, cerebrovascular, renal, and visual end-organ damage.
Reviews smoking, alcohol, diet, weight, exercise, and occupational/psychosocial stress.
Explicitly explores mood and erectile function and connects this to drug choice.
Explains hypertension is controllable but generally lifelong, without inventing false certainty.
Selects the correct first-line drug class by the supplied age/ethnicity rule.
Explains stepped add-on therapy (A+C, then +D) if control is not achieved.
Gives class-specific side-effect counselling, avoiding or flagging beta-blocker/diuretic effects on mood and sexual function.
Arranges baseline investigations, follow-up interval, and safety-netting for new symptoms.

globalRating: Clear fail — Unsafe, disorganised, or unable to achieve the core task despite prompts.
Borderline — Partial achievement with important omissions; may require prompts but avoids major harm.
Pass — Safe, structured, clinically appropriate performance with minor omissions.
Good — Efficient, patient-centred, well-reasoned performance with clear prioritisation.
Excellent — Fluent integration of clinical reasoning, communication, safety-netting, and context without irrelevant overreach.
promptQuestions: "Which drug class would you avoid given his mood and erectile-function concerns, and why?"
"What determines the first-line drug choice in this patient?"
"What baseline tests would you arrange before and during treatment?"
criticalSafetyErrors: Chooses a first-line drug that contradicts the supplied age/ethnicity rule without justification.
Ignores the mood/erectile-dysfunction history when selecting therapy.
Fails to screen for secondary causes or end-organ damage before starting treatment.

stations.title: Atrial Fibrillation
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history, stroke-risk assessment, and rate/rhythm/anticoagulation decision-making
candidateInstructions: An adult presents with palpitations and an irregularly irregular pulse, newly confirmed as atrial fibrillation on ECG.

In 10 minutes: take a focused history, interpret the supplied risk-factor summary, explain the CHA2DS2-VASc-style stroke-risk approach, and outline the anticoagulation, rate-control, and (where relevant) rhythm-control plan.
Do not quote a specific anticoagulant dose; discuss the decision at the class/strategy level.
candidateHandout: History: palpitations for several weeks, intermittent, with mild breathlessness on exertion; no syncope, no chest pain at rest.
Risk factors present: hypertension (treated), age over 65, no diabetes, no prior stroke/TIA, no vascular disease, sex as supplied by faculty for local scoring convention.
Examination: irregularly irregular pulse around 100–110/min; no signs of heart failure; BP controlled.
learningNotes: Learning note: NICE NG196 supports a structured stroke-risk assessment (CHA2DS2-VASc-based) before starting anticoagulation, weighed against bleeding risk factors; most patients with a meaningful stroke-risk score benefit from anticoagulation regardless of whether rate or rhythm control is chosen for symptom control. Rate control (commonly a beta-blocker) is first-line for most patients; rhythm control (cardioversion, antiarrhythmics, or ablation) is considered for symptomatic patients, new-onset AF, or where rate control fails. Anticoagulation decisions are not deferred just because rhythm control is planned.
simulationScript: Opening: "Doctor, my heart has been racing on and off for a few weeks, and I get a bit breathless."

If asked: no fainting, no chest pain at rest, no leg swelling; hypertension is treated and usually well-controlled; no known diabetes, stroke, or vascular disease; drinks alcohol occasionally; no excess caffeine.
If asked about bleeding risk: no history of bleeding, no liver or kidney disease, not on other blood-thinning or anti-inflammatory medicine, alcohol intake is modest.
ICE: worried this means a stroke is inevitable; wants to know if the heart can be "fixed" back to normal rhythm; anxious about being on blood thinners long term.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. Do not require a specific numeric CHA2DS2-VASc score to be calculated aloud if the candidate correctly identifies and weighs the relevant risk factors (age, hypertension, sex, absence of diabetes/stroke/vascular disease).

Full marks require the candidate to state that anticoagulation is generally indicated given the risk-factor burden, independent of the rate-vs-rhythm decision, and to weigh bleeding risk factors before committing.
Accept any safe locally available anticoagulant class discussion (a DOAC or a vitamin-K antagonist with monitoring) without requiring a specific drug name or dose. Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Take a focused history covering onset, triggers, associated syncope/chest pain, breathlessness, and known risk factors for stroke and bleeding.

Confirm AF from the irregularly irregular pulse and ECG, and structure a CHA2DS2-VASc-style risk assessment (age, hypertension, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA, vascular disease, sex) against a bleeding-risk assessment.

Explain that most patients with a meaningful stroke-risk burden should be anticoagulated regardless of the rate/rhythm strategy chosen, and discuss anticoagulant options at a class level with monitoring/bleeding safety-netting.

candidateInstructions: Mrs Saira Iqbal, aged 63 years, has known heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and is reviewed in clinic with worsening breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling.

candidateHandout: Known heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (confirmed by echocardiogram at diagnosis). Currently breathless walking one flight of stairs (previously two); bilateral ankle swelling; weight increased by 2 kg in a week; sleeps on two pillows.

stations.title: Acute Pulmonary Oedema
stations.primaryCompetency: Emergency recognition and protocol-based treatment of acute decompensated heart failure
candidateInstructions: You are called to an adult with known heart disease who has sudden severe breathlessness, cannot lie flat, and is coughing pink frothy sputum.
In 10 minutes: lead immediate assessment and management. Verbalise all orders to the nurse/examiner.
Do not delay treatment to complete a full history.
candidateHandout: A–E: airway patent; breathing rapid and laboured with bilateral crackles to the mid-zones and audible wheeze; oxygen saturation low on air; circulation shows tachycardia and elevated blood pressure; alert but anxious and unable to speak in full sentences.
learningNotes: Learning note: Acute pulmonary oedema needs the patient sat upright, high-flow oxygen to correct hypoxia, IV loop diuretic (e.g. furosemide), and, if BP allows, a nitrate infusion/spray to reduce preload. Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP) is used for persistent hypoxia/respiratory distress despite initial treatment under local protocol. Identify and treat the precipitant (ischaemia, arrhythmia, uncontrolled hypertension, valve failure, non-adherence). Caution is needed if the patient is hypotensive — nitrates and excessive diuresis can worsen a low-output state, which needs a different approach (inotropic support) under specialist guidance.

After sitting upright, oxygen, and IV furosemide are ordered: state saturation begins to improve, breathing remains laboured.

Escalate to a CPAP/non-invasive ventilation discussion and senior/ICU involvement if the candidate asks about ongoing hypoxia despite initial treatment.

Give an IV loop diuretic and reassess; give a nitrate infusion/spray if blood pressure is adequate, avoiding it (and cautious with diuresis) if the patient is hypotensive.
Consider CPAP/non-invasive ventilation for persistent hypoxia or distress under local protocol, and escalate for possible inotropic support if a low-output/hypotensive picture emerges.

Reversible causes (drugs such as beta-blockers/calcium-channel blockers/digoxin, electrolyte disturbance, ischaemia) should be sought and corrected in parallel.

stations.title: Supraventricular Tachycardia
stations.primaryCompetency: Emergency recognition and stepwise treatment of narrow-complex tachycardia
candidateInstructions: An adult presents with sudden-onset palpitations and a regular, fast, narrow-complex rhythm on the monitor. The patient is talking normally and alert.
In 10 minutes: lead assessment and stepwise management, verbalising all actions and orders to the nurse/examiner.

candidateHandout: A–E: airway patent; breathing normal; heart rate very fast and regular, narrow QRS on monitor; blood pressure currently adequate; patient alert, mildly anxious, able to converse in full sentences.

learningNotes: Learning note: Stable narrow-complex SVT is managed per the Resuscitation Council UK/ESC tachycardia approach: vagal manoeuvres first (e.g. modified Valsalva, carotid sinus massage only if no bruit and locally appropriate), then IV adenosine as a rapid bolus with a flush, escalating the dose if the first is ineffective, with continuous ECG recording during administration. If adverse features (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, heart failure) are present or the rhythm fails to respond and the patient deteriorates, synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation/anaesthesia is required without delay. Adenosine is avoided or used with extreme caution in patients with asthma/reactive airway disease and pre-excitation with atrial fibrillation.

If asked: no chest pain, no fainting, no known heart disease; no asthma; first episode like this.

After adenosine ordered: ask the candidate to specify continuous ECG recording during administration; state the rhythm terminates (or, if the candidate is being tested on escalation, state it recurs/fails to terminate after the correct stepwise doses — follow local station-specific branch as instructed by faculty).
If adverse features are introduced (chest pain, falling BP, reduced consciousness) and the candidate does not move to synchronised cardioversion: provide the emergency stall prompt.

stations.title: Infective Endocarditis
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history, examination, and referral planning for suspected endocarditis
candidateInstructions: An adult with a known heart-valve abnormality presents with several weeks of low-grade fever and general malaise.
In 10 minutes: take a focused history, describe a focused examination for the peripheral stigmata of endocarditis, interpret the supplied findings, and outline the investigation and referral pathway.

candidateHandout: History: fatigue, low-grade intermittent fever, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss over several weeks; known rheumatic mitral valve disease from childhood; no recent dental or skin procedure reported yet (ask directly).

Examination findings on request: a new or changed heart murmur, low-grade fever, splinter haemorrhages, and tender nodules on the finger pulps (Osler's nodes); no obvious skin abscess or IV drug use track marks.
learningNotes: Learning note: Suspected infective endocarditis needs blood cultures (at least three sets from different sites before any antibiotic) and echocardiography (transthoracic first-line, transoesophageal if non-diagnostic or high clinical suspicion), interpreted alongside the modified Duke criteria (major criteria include positive blood cultures typical for endocarditis and evidence of endocardial involvement on imaging; minor criteria include predisposing heart condition, fever, vascular/immunological phenomena). Empirical antibiotics should not be started before cultures are taken unless the patient is septic/haemodynamically unstable, and antibiotic choice is a specialist/microbiology-guided decision. NICE CG64 addresses antibiotic prophylaxis before interventional procedures in at-risk patients as a separate, distinct topic from treatment of established disease.

If asked: known childhood rheumatic heart disease affecting a valve; had a dental extraction about a month before symptoms began; no IV drug use; no recent skin infection or piercing.
If asked about symptoms: night sweats, unintentional weight loss, joint aches, no cough, no urinary symptoms, no rash other than what is found on examination.
If asked for examination: as per handout — new/changed murmur, low-grade fever, splinter haemorrhages, tender finger-pulp nodules; no signs of embolic stroke or acute limb ischaemia currently.
ICE: worried this is "just a virus" and reluctant to be admitted; concerned about missing work.

Do not require an antibiotic regimen to be named — expect referral to hospital/cardiology-microbiology for culture-guided treatment. Prompted items score at most 1/2.

Structure the diagnosis using the modified Duke criteria (major: positive blood cultures typical of endocarditis, echocardiographic/imaging evidence of endocardial involvement; minor: predisposing condition, fever, vascular and immunological phenomena, microbiological evidence not meeting major criteria).

Take at least three sets of blood cultures from different sites before starting any antibiotic (unless the patient is septic/unstable), and arrange echocardiography (transthoracic first, transoesophageal if needed).

Refer urgently for specialist (cardiology/microbiology, often via hospital admission) culture-guided antibiotic therapy rather than starting empirical treatment in this setting; discuss the separate, distinct role of antibiotic prophylaxis before future at-risk procedures.

stations.primaryCompetency: Emergency recognition, risk stratification, and protocol-based treatment
candidateInstructions: An adult develops sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain three days after major surgery.

candidateHandout: A–E: airway patent; breathing rapid with pleuritic chest pain, oxygen saturation low on air; circulation shows tachycardia; blood pressure currently borderline-low; patient anxious, mild lightheadedness.
Post-operative day 3 after major abdominal surgery; limited mobility since surgery; no bleeding or anticoagulant contraindication reported.
learningNotes: Learning note: High clinical suspicion of PE with haemodynamic compromise (hypotension or shock) is treated as high-risk and needs immediate resuscitation, oxygen, and urgent senior/critical-care involvement, with consideration of thrombolysis if confirmed or strongly suspected and imaging is not immediately possible in a deteriorating patient — do not wait for a formal Wells/PESI calculation to give oxygen and call for help. In a haemodynamically stable patient, risk-stratify with the Wells score / clinical probability, obtain CT pulmonary angiography (or V/Q scan if contraindicated), and start anticoagulation without delay while awaiting confirmation if clinical suspicion is high. Postoperative VTE prophylaxis omission and immobility are the relevant precipitants here and should prompt review of the thromboprophylaxis plan going forward.

candidateInstructions: An adult with a childhood history of rheumatic fever presents with progressive breathlessness and occasional palpitations.

candidateHandout: History: childhood history of rheumatic fever with recurrent sore throats; progressive breathlessness on exertion over recent months; occasional palpitations; no chest pain; no haemoptysis currently.

Examination on request: a malar flush, irregularly irregular pulse (in keeping with atrial fibrillation), a loud first heart sound with an opening snap, and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur best heard at the apex in the left lateral position; no signs of pulmonary oedema at present.
learningNotes: Learning note: Rheumatic mitral stenosis commonly presents with exertional breathlessness, and atrial fibrillation is a common and important complication because of left atrial enlargement, itself increasing thromboembolic stroke risk substantially. Management under the ESC/EACTS 2021 valvular heart disease guideline includes rate control and anticoagulation for associated AF, monitoring for pulmonary hypertension/right heart failure, and referral for consideration of balloon valvuloplasty or surgical valve intervention once symptoms or valve severity warrant it. Secondary antibiotic prophylaxis against recurrent rheumatic fever, and endocarditis-prophylaxis counselling for future at-risk procedures, remain relevant in patients with a rheumatic history.

stations.title: Dyslipidaemia

candidateHandout: Results: total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol above the laboratory reference range; HDL cholesterol low-normal; triglycerides mildly raised.

stations.title: Cardiac Arrest
stations.primaryCompetency: Basic and advanced life support: recognition, CPR quality, and rhythm-directed treatment
candidateInstructions: You find an adult collapsed and unresponsive on the ward corridor.
In 10 minutes: lead recognition and resuscitation using a basic-life-support-into-advanced-life-support sequence, verbalising every action and order to the team/examiner.
Manikin and simulated monitor/defibrillator are available; verbalise all interventions clearly.
candidateHandout: Initial state: unresponsive, not breathing normally, no signs of life on brief check.
Once CPR/monitor are attached: first rhythm shown is shockable (ventricular fibrillation).
learningNotes: Learning note: The Resuscitation Council UK 2021 adult ALS algorithm begins with confirming unresponsiveness and absent normal breathing, shouting for help, and starting high-quality chest compressions (rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, full recoil, minimal interruption) with asynchronous ventilations once an airway adjunct is placed. Attach a monitor/defibrillator as soon as available. For a shockable rhythm (VF/pulseless VT): give one shock immediately, resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes without a rhythm/pulse check, then reassess; give adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO after the third shock and every 3–5 minutes thereafter, and amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO after the third shock (further dose after the fifth if still in a shockable rhythm). For a non-shockable rhythm (asystole/PEA): give adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO as soon as access is obtained and every 3–5 minutes, continuing CPR with rhythm checks every 2 minutes. Identify and treat reversible causes (the 4 Hs and 4 Ts: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia and other metabolic abnormalities, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thromboembolism) throughout.
simulationScript: Examiner/nurse cues: on approach, state "the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally" once the candidate checks.

When a monitor/defibrillator is attached: state the rhythm is shockable (VF).

After the shock and 2 minutes of CPR: state the rhythm remains shockable on the second check unless the candidate has otherwise correctly requested a reassessment cadence, in which case follow the standard 2-minute-cycle branching per local mock-code convention.

If compressions are interrupted for longer than necessary (e.g. prolonged pauses to "feel for a pulse" during a cycle) or a shock is delayed: provide the emergency stall prompt and note this for scoring.

If asked about reversible causes: provide simulated findings as directed by faculty (e.g. no obvious external bleeding, normal-looking chest wall) to allow the candidate to verbalise the 4H/4T screen.
examinerInstructions: Run this as a structured mock code. Expect an immediate, confident BLS opening (unresponsive/breathing check, shout for help/activate emergency response, start compressions) before any equipment is available.

Full marks require correct compression rate/depth as verbalised or demonstrated, minimal hands-off time, correct shock-then-immediate-CPR sequence, correctly timed adrenaline (after the third shock in a shockable rhythm; immediately in a non-shockable rhythm) and amiodarone (after the third shock), and an explicit 4H/4T reversible-cause screen.
Prompted items score at most 1/2. A dangerous pause in compressions or a missed/delayed shock is a critical safety error regardless of other performance.
keyAnswerGuide: Confirm unresponsiveness and absent normal breathing quickly; shout for help/activate the emergency response; start high-quality chest compressions immediately (rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, full recoil, minimal interruption), with ventilations once airway support is available.

Attach the monitor/defibrillator as soon as possible and recognise the shockable rhythm; deliver one shock, then resume CPR immediately for a full 2-minute cycle without checking rhythm or pulse in between.

Give adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO after the third shock and repeat every 3–5 minutes; give amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO after the third shock (a further 150 mg dose may be given after the fifth shock if still shockable).
If the rhythm becomes non-shockable (asystole/PEA), continue CPR with adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO as soon as access is obtained and every 3–5 minutes, without shocks.

Throughout, systematically consider and address the 4 Hs (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia/metabolic, hypothermia) and 4 Ts (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thromboembolism); minimise hands-off time at every rhythm check and maintain clear team communication and role allocation.

Give adrenaline and amiodarone at the correct timing.
Minimise hands-off time throughout.
